newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG mercenaries only interested in mine, says general.
newsitem.headline: PNG mercenaries only interested in mine, says general.

text.p: Mercenaries hired to put down a secessionist rebellion in Papua New Guinea planned to capture a vast copper mine on Bougainville island with a force of 1,200 soldiers, a public inquiry was told on Wednesday.

Sacked army commander Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok told the inquiry into last month's aborted mercenary operation that British-based military consultancy Sandline International wanted to make the mine the focus of its operation.

Hired by the PNG government to help put down the nine-year rebellion on Bougainville island, Sandline wanted to change its plans and concentrate on the Panguna mine after its US$36 million contract with the government became public.

"The new concept was, instead of heavily engaging military operations in central Bougainville ... to deploy a battalion-size group on the Panguna mine and then let the rebels come and fight with us around the mine," Singirok said.
The new plan would involve 800 soldiers and 400 support staff, he said.

Singirok also said he told the Sandline chief executive, retired British colonel Tim Spicer, that it would be difficult to raise a force of that size and that capturing the mine should not have been the main priority.

The inquiry heard last week that Sandline had proposed a venture with the PNG government and the mine's owners to operate the mine after it was reopened. Spicer told the inquiry this plan had not been taken seriously by the PNG government.
The Panguna mine, operated by Australian mining giant RTZ-CRA, was closed in May 1989 after a series of sabotage attacks by rebels on the island 800 km (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby.
At the time it supplied a third of PNG's foreign exchange.

Sandline signed the contract with the PNG government in January to supply 70 African soldiers and weapons, including two Russian-made helicopter gunships, for an assault against the Bougainville rebels.

But Singirok led an army rebellion against the mercenaries in March and forced prime minister Sir Julius Chan and two senior ministers to stand down pending an inquiry into the deal. Either Chan or defence minister Mathias Ijape, who also stood aside, were expected to be called by the inquiry after Singirok completed his evidence on Thursday.
Singirok also said he was concerned about what Spicer planned to do with US$400,000 he brought into the country.
"I have got serious doubts about the reason for that money to be brought into the country," he said. "It could be related to claims of money being used for corrupt purposes."
The money was confiscated by rebel soldiers and handed to the inquiry by Singirok on Tuesday.
Singirok also told the inquiry the prime minister's department wanted to take over the army's Rapid Reaction Force and use it in conjunction with police to form a "palace guard".

"Palace guard is a loose military description of private armies run by Third World countries ... to give personal protection to the politicians whilst rendering the legitimate defence force unoperational," he said.

Spicer left Port Moresby on Tuesday after a court agreed to drop illegal firearms charges against him. He had been held in the South Pacific nation's capital since being detained on March 16 by rebel army officers, who also threw his 70 African mercenaries out of the South Pacific country.
